sections.title: Woord Vooraf In Memoriam (p.2)
sections.text: FOREWORD In your hands, you have the Yearbook of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2022. In this, you can read about the deployments the navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, as well as the actions taken by the shore organization to facilitate these deployments. Although some COVID-19 measures were still in place at the beginning of the year, the government gradually lifted these restrictions, allowing for more activities. Thus, exercises and events could continue, and normalcy returned. The Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) once again made a significant impression during the Navy Days in Den Helder. Additionally, this year saw Velas Latinoamérica Curaçao, a unique celebration featuring several tall ships visiting Willemstad. The KM was also represented there. With many visitors, it was a great success and a wonderful opportunity to showcase what the KM has to offer. The personnel underwent many new trainings, courses, and participated in (international) exercises. At the World Port Days in Rotterdam, the navy was present with marines and ships to introduce visitors to the naval forces. We hope that this Yearbook will once again prove to be a useful reference work. Editorial Team Yearbooks Royal Netherlands Navy Foreword Commander of Naval Forces Vice Admiral R.P. Tas.

sections.text: 3_Navy_Annual_Report_2022_ORGANIZATION_OVERVIEWS-7 18 Organization Overviews Finance and Control (F&C) Head: Captain (ktz) drs. J.F. Kwak, acting head from April 18 to July 12 K. van der Maas, from July 12 drs. T.R. Timmerman The F&C department carried out its tasks, namely supporting C-ZSK by providing preparation, execution, progress, and quality of financial policy advice, compiling the budget and establishing the expenditure program, executing financial management as well as contributing to information provision with management and steering reports and preparing the cash forecast quarterly. Whereas in previous years the budgetary space was limited and sometimes strategic choices had to be made or even restrictions had to be imposed on budget execution, this was not necessary in the budget year 2022 due to the allocation of additional resources and commitments from the coalition agreement. Starting in 2022, the department made the coast guards visible as a separate budget item in the budget. This allows F&C to better distinguish the performance and results of the three organizations. The resources promised in the coalition agreement and in the measures note starting from 2023 and subsequent years had a positive effect on the implementation of the plans in 2022. Due to national and global shortages of goods and services and tightness in the labor market, production capacity at C-ZSK still lagged behind in 2022.

sections.title: Organisatieoverzichten (p.9)
sections.text: Organizational Overviews In 2022, CZSK (Royal Netherlands Navy Command) spent a net € 101 million more on personnel expenses than was included in the draft budget. The cause of this is primarily due to additional expenses resulting from the collective labor agreement 2021-2023, temporary salary structure allowances, and increased compensation for pension costs. Due to underfilling of permanent staff, expenditures for hiring temporary workers and consultants for operational management and IT were higher than anticipated. This hiring was necessary to procure essential personnel in order to prevent stagnation in the execution of the Navy's tasks as much as possible. In 2022, CZSK received € 3.3 million more in the operational budget than was included in the draft budget. This was mainly caused by a higher contribution from the countries to the Caribbean Coast Guard (catching up on backlog) from previous years. Defense Materiel Fund (DMF) In the DMF, expenditures in 2022 were higher than the budget allocated at the beginning of the year (€ 155 million) plus additional allocations (€ 97 million). However, due to a budget (€ 83 million) being deferred to 2026 through a cash shift, a surplus of € 33 million was presented as of December 31. This is mainly due to a higher reliability of delivery of goods and services than was estimated at the time of the cash shift, resulting in more being realized. The budget shifted to 2026 can be used to cover potential future shortfalls in the DMF. Additionally, within the fund in 2022, € 13.4 million more was received due to extra efforts in collecting overdue invoices. This includes CZSK catching up from previous years (e.g., maintenance on Portuguese M-frigates) and, in net terms, higher incidental VAT receipts. These extra receipts are and will be used for the maintenance of maritime materiel.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.3)
sections.text: The Directorate of Personnel and Organization of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) must always have sufficient, well-qualified, and motivated personnel available to carry out its tasks. For 2022, the focal points of the directorate were: Improving the space for tailored agreements, where protocols are guiding but not leading. Developing opportunities for additional capacity such as alternative recruitment and flexible use of labor market potential. Intensifying collaboration with the Personnel Logistics Service Center, the business community, knowledge institutions, the province of North Holland, and employment agencies for the purpose of recruitment. Developing, in addition to a core of well-trained personnel with long-term contracts, a flexible layer by utilizing various contract forms in an open personnel system. Knowledge building and knowledge retention are anchored through career paths and longer job durations. Marines during a night exercise near Dordrecht.

The department advises and supports CZSK, the directors of CZSK, and commanders of units on all legal issues that arise. JUZA provides legal advice and acts as a point of contact for the directors and commanders within CZSK. Additionally, JUZA monitors the legal and administrative diligence of operations within CZSK. The main areas of law that the department deals with include (military) criminal and disciplinary law, operational law, and state and administrative law. These areas of law are organized into three different offices. Thus, every employee at JUZA can serve as the first point of contact (counter function) for questions directed to the department. JUZA does not provide legal advice to individual military personnel but does assist them if necessary. In criminal or disciplinary matters, JUZA is primarily involved on the side of CZSK and Defense as an organization. If a military member is involved in a criminal case, they can receive assistance from Defense in that matter.

Within the various departments, they drew lessons from the operational management they employed during the past period and the use of remote working. Over the past year, several teams were active simultaneously. This approach allows for better application of the principles of BGO in developing the core and sub-tasks in the O&iT proposals. An L&D officer oversees the office, which consists of three staff members. The new colleagues first completed several training courses at the ECOD. Last year, it was noted that the backlog of qualified trainers was significant. In the afternoon, they invited participants to develop their own lessons and then discuss them with them. The workshop met a need and will be repeated in 2023. The Education Innovation office has three staff members supplemented by several MBO students who are doing internships there. Pul Head of Integrated Security Staff Office: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) (SD) J. van Rijn In November 2019, the Directorate of Integrated Operations & Governance (IB&B) was established. The aim of this consolidation of departments focused on operations and governance within the CZSK was: to achieve greater integration and effectiveness in operations and governance; to provide improved management of the safety organization; to realize a better distribution of the workload within the various directorates of CZSK. From December 2020 to March 2021, the directorate conducted an evaluation. One of the conclusions was that the above objectives had not been fully achieved. This has various causes. At the establishment of the directorate, it was based on the existing structures. At that time, no organizational improvements were made other than an administrative reorganization. The intended synergy between the different departments was not yet fully achieved through this reorganization. Additionally, the Governance Staff initiated various developments in recent years that directly impacted the organization of the IB&B directorate. This includes the establishment of the CIO system, the embedding of Portfolio and Program Management (P3O), the strengthening of short-cycle innovation, and the strengthening of Safety and Environment (V&M). As a result of the introduction of the new top structure within Defense, the interfaces between the directorate and the Governance Staff also changed. For effective realization of the objectives, it was necessary to logically cluster the tasks. This clustering had to align with BBD2020 and DN 2022.

In this way, a decisive, future-oriented organization emerged with the capacity for change to contribute to the further development of the CZSK. This was followed by a SARC-4 period from March 14 to March 25 in the North Sea in international exercise areas. During the weekend, there was also a port visit to the British coastal town of Portsmouth. In preparation for the safe crossing of Zr.Ms. Groningen to the West, the ship conducted a CT from April 4 to April 8 in the North Sea. Given the satisfactory result, the status Ready For Sea was reaffirmed, and the ship could cross to the Caribbean. Here, Zr.Ms. Groningen conducted a PDT with the STC staff from April 23 to April 29. At the end, the staff declared the ship 'mission specific ready,' allowing it to commence its counter-drug operations, among other tasks. From May 9 to May 20, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam underwent a CT period in the North Sea, the Kattegat, and the North Sea. Apart from various training sessions, including a disaster exercise in a Danish training village, the ship made a port visit to the Swedish city of Gothenburg. Sustaining operational readiness proved not yet possible, and the ship received the status Ready For Sea. The last training effort of the STC staff and personnel before the summer leave was a CT/PDT on Zr.Ms. Groningen in the West. During the period from July 5 to July 13, they carried out an intensive program off the coast near Willemstad. After the concluding patrol exercise, which included various exercise incidents and the interception of a smuggling vessel, C-STC again declared the ship 'mission specific ready' for counter-drug operations. After the summer leave, from September 6 to September 15, the interim training of Zr.Ms. Rotterdam continued with a second CT. At the end of this period, readiness increased by identifying points of attention and making the necessary next steps.

After the first of two weeks of training, the ship also made a port visit to the southern English city. During the training, the crew made upward progress, and STC was able to assign the status of 'operationally ready.' Zr.Ms. Van Amstel was thus prepared for its SNMG task at the beginning of 2023. sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2022_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-38 99 Operations Directorate Maritime Warfare Centre (MWC) Head: Colonel (ltkolmarns) J. de Wolf The year 2022 was primarily focused on rebalancing for the MWC, restoring balance after the pandemic. This involved restructuring part of the capacity to better meet the demands of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK). It led to the establishment of a Subject Matter Expert (SME) for Maritime Unmanned & Autonomous Systems, the creation of an additional SME for Anti-Submarine Warfare (VTE filled after four years of vacancy), and the merging of capabilities for Maritime Ballistic Missile Defence and Above Water Warfare. This did come at the expense of the VTE SME Operational Technology, which means that CZSK must draw on expertise elsewhere for the Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear dossier. Driven by personnel shortages, the centre must apply a more forced and sharper delineation of tasks. The MWC's core task is to support the Force Development of the operational navy broadly, developing the contemporary navy into the navy of tomorrow. The focus is on practical support at a low-tactical level with a conceptual approach. Strategic issues are primarily addressed in The Hague and at S&A, while hard technology development is mainly the responsibility of the Defence Materiel Organization (DMO), with the understanding that the MWC remains in continuous consultation with the aforementioned departments. However, the centre also continues to work on a strong network of knowledge partners. The rebalancing here mainly involves re-establishing contacts that were lost during COVID-19. The external pressure on the MWC as a knowledge provider increased significantly this year. Due to the growing tensions in the world, the Defence budget steadily rose, creating more opportunities for new projects, as well as expansion, re-evaluation, and/or acceleration of ongoing investment projects. Wherever maritime capacity review was concerned, Defence called upon the MWC to provide capacity and expertise to support planning. At the same time, more regular (inter)national meetings could again be organized physically. This was done extensively to restore ties between various knowledge parties. Vernède After its annual maintenance at Van der Hoeven Shipyard in Drimmelen, the ship began the sailing season 2022 in the last week of March. This sailing week was the last week for Lieutenant 1st Class (ltz1) E. de Jonge as commander of Zr.Ms. Urania. Upon arrival in its home port, the command transfer took place on April 1st. From this day, Lieutenant 1st Class (ltz1) V. Vernède took command of the sailing ship. After its annual material trials and preparations, the season started with the Race of the Classics, which took place from April 18th to April 24th. During this race, working students from Defensity College participated as crew members. After the event, the ship proceeded to Enkhuizen for two weeks of relationship sailing days. After a short stop in Den Helder, the training program for the cadets and officers in training began. This year, the sailing area was chosen to be the West Coast of France and Belgium, the Norwegian Fjords, the Swedish Archipelago, and the Baltic Sea. In addition to the training character of this period, Zr.Ms. Urania also participated in events in Ostend and anchored in Kiel for the Kieler Woche. The summer was marked for the ship by participation in the Tall Ships Races. This annual sailing event attracts dozens of ships, which compete in various races to different European ports. This year, Zr.Ms. Urania started the race in Esbjerg. During the race to Harlingen, the sailing ship encountered various weather conditions, ranging from calms to wind force six. After this first race, Zr.Ms. Urania participated in SAIL Harlingen with the Tall Ships fleet. The second leg of the Tall Ships Races consisted of the Cruise in Company from Harlingen to Antwerp. During this leg, Zr.Ms. Urania took the initiative to explore the IJsselmeer with the ships with (relatively) shallow draft. This led to a convoy of twelve vessels that jointly lay in the lock and entered Enkhuizen with a sail-in parade. sections.title: Directie Materiële Instandh (p.20)
sections.text: Directorate of Material Maintenance Deployment Each year, Zr.Ms. Van Kinsbergen sails for approximately 200 days. The main user is the Royal Netherlands Naval College (KIM). The ship is deployed to teach future naval officers (adelborsten) practical nautical skills. These skills are necessary to work as a watch officer on the bridge of a naval vessel. The vessel serves as a supplement to theory and (bridge) simulator lessons. Future navigation officers receive various training on board, such as mooring and unmooring. Additionally, the ship also has a formative function, including team building and character development. Besides the KIM, the Dutch-Belgian Operational School is also a major user. Students at the OPSCHOOL receive practical sailing training for the qualifications of non-commissioned officers for minehunters, hydrographic survey vessels, and submarines. Civil Maritime Schools The civil maritime school on Terschelling, the Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz (MIWB), also makes good use of Zr.Ms. Van Kinsbergen for training future maritime officers. Within the framework of the agreement, the MIWB has access to the training vessel for several weeks. Second-year Maritime Officer students undertake short practical trips on this ship. During their stay on board, navigation is particularly practiced. Additionally, the MIWB uses the ship for Advanced Fire Fighting training, where realistic emergency scenarios are practiced on board. Instructors from the MIWB provide lessons for the adelborsten of the KIM in Den Helder. These lessons cover subjects such as loading technology and maritime law. Within the agreement, there is an exploration of how to expand cooperation to further modernize and improve education within both institutions. Scientific Research Upon request, bridge teams from individual ships can use Zr.Ms. Van Kinsbergen for tailored training or as part of a training program. Occasionally, the ship is used for scientific research (TNO and universities) or for informational purposes. Two Crews Zr.Ms. Van Kinsbergen has two crews of five persons each; a military and a civilian crew. The latter consists of a captain, a first and a second mate, a chief engineer, and a cook. The military crew consists of a commander (kltz), a senior officer, a skipper with sailing qualifications, a chief technical officer, and a cook.

sections.text: Directie Materiële Instandhouding Zeedienst Practicum (ZPR) 1 For the first sailing period of 2022, the MOV was deployed for the KIM for the so-called ZPR1. In this practicum, the leadership establishes a foundation for safe (visual) navigation in combination with GPS and traditional nautical charts from point A to point B. This is the first sailing period for the cadets aboard the Van Kinsbergen. This journey lasted four weeks and was with the Zeedienst intake year 21. This period was from January 27 to February 23. The ship began its journey with high hopes, but the crew soon faced several setbacks. The so-called Delta variant of COVID-19 spread rapidly worldwide, and unfortunately, the crew and personnel of the Van Kinsbergen could no longer fend off the virus. Despite the measures taken, the ship was forced to return to Den Helder and adjust the sailing program. The weather was also uncooperative during this time of year. Storms Dudley, Eunice, and Franklin swept over the MOV, causing multiple schoolings in various ports, and the sailing area was later even restricted to only the Wadden Sea and the roadstead of Den Helder. Storm Eunice ranks among the top three heaviest storms in over fifty years. Other voyages From March 13 to March 18, the Van Kinsbergen sailed for a week for the MIWB. During this time, the ship made day trips from Terschelling and moored in the evening at West-Terschelling. Afterwards, the Van Kinsbergen sailed from March 21 to March 31 for DVS for the ZeeWachtStandaard-K course in the Baltic Sea. During this period, the crew conducted various navigation exercises to train the students and prepare them for their Practical Business Introduction to the fleet. At the beginning of April, the ship sailed again for the MIWB. The Van Kinsbergen served during this period as a platform for the Advanced Fire Fighting training courses, where realistic emergency scenarios are practiced on board. ZPR 2 From April 21 to May 27, the Van Kinsbergen sailed again for the KIM with the cadets of Z21. During this period, the lost time from their first period, which for some was disrupted by the pandemic, had to be made up. The students picked up where they left off, and a new aspect for the cadet came into play: navigating with the help of radar in combination with visual observation. Fortunately, COVID-19 did not interfere this time, and the crew was able to complete the program in its entirety. Philipse-Breitenstein Mission The mission of CZMCARIB is derived from the mission of CZSK and translates to the environment in the West as: 'Providing security in the Caribbean.' This one sentence articulates what CZMCARIB stands for and focuses at the strategic level on the realization of the three main tasks of defense in the Caribbean: Protecting the integrity and interests of the territory of Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB is responsible for the territorial integrity of the Caribbean countries of the Kingdom and Caribbean Netherlands. The own and visiting operational units have a so-called threshold function. This means that through our presence and our activities, we have a deterrent effect against potential hostilities from foreign countries or organizations. Promoting the international rule of law and stability. The second main task also includes deployment for international law enforcement, such as combating the smuggling of weapons and drugs by sea. CZMCARIB promotes regional security and stability by, among other things, carrying out

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.3)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean for counter illicit trafficking operations and through international military cooperation. The United States and France are the main international partners in this regard. C-ZMCARIB fulfills the CIT task as Commander Task Group 4.4 (CTG 4.4), a subordinate commander of the American Joint Interagency Task Force South. The support of civil authorities. The Dutch Armed Forces have developed into a structural security partner within the Kingdom. The armed forces now have broader support capabilities with their highly developed specialist and unique capabilities. CZMCARIB provides units that can be deployed for military assistance to Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB also provides support to third parties, primarily to the Coast Guard in the Caribbean (KWCARIB). C-ZMCARIB is also the Director of KWCARIB. It also provides emergency aid during disasters and crises. Finally, CZMCARIB also supports the Social Development Programs in Curaçao and Aruba. Vision To realize the mission of CZMCARIB as adequately as possible in light of the surrounding changes, a vision has been established. The vision of CZMCARIB is: ‘CZMCARIB is the relevant maritime and security partner in the Caribbean, as part of the CZSK.’ Arrival of Zr.Ms. Friesland in Willemstad.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.4)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean This means that CZMCARIB aims to be recognized as the obvious and reliable partner when it comes to contributing to security in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom. 'Relevant maritime' and 'security partner' in the above vision refers to the fact that CZMCARIB assigns a high priority to the second and third primary tasks. Due to national and international agreements, it aims to promote the international and local rule of law with its own resources, for example by contributing capabilities to (inter)national organizations or by providing military assistance. Reflection on 2022 With the global decline of the pandemic, activities in the CARIB (both military and civilian) gradually gained momentum. The number of training activities in the CARIB as a training hub increased throughout the year, as did the participation of its own units in exercises elsewhere in the region. This provided a positive boost to operational readiness. On February 24, Russia invaded Ukraine. Just as in the Netherlands, the Alert State was raised in the West, a situation that was maintained throughout the year. Additionally, in mid-2022, Velas Latino America Curaçao (VLAC) 2022 took place. A large sailing event, comparable to SAIL Amsterdam. CZMCARIB was closely involved in the preparations and was represented during the event with a defense village where Defense presented itself, including Caribbean military personnel and the Company in the West (CidW). Zr.Ms. Dolfijn and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan also made their presence known. International Drug Enforcement In addition to the external defense of six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, Defense plays an important role in upholding the international rule of law in the Caribbean region. Given the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The navy is thus closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization Joint Interagency Task Force South in Key West. The Commander (kltz) of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is therefore the commander of Taskgroup 4.4., one of the task groups of this organization.

sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean SSCG was under the command of C-ZMCARIB. Until April, Zr.Ms. Friesland fulfilled this role, after which Zr.Ms. Groningen arrived as a relief in the same month. Zr.Ms. Holland relieved her in October. The SSCG did not have access to an NH90 this year. Therefore, for the duration of two rotations, the collaboration established in 2014 with the United States Coast Guard's Helicopter Interdiction Tactical Squadron continued. During these rotations, an MH-65 helicopter was embarked on board. In addition to the regular cooperation with the Dash-8 of the Caribbean Coast Guard, the SSCG had air support from the Dutch MQ-9 of 306 Squadron of CLSK this year. This improved aerial coverage was experienced by the SSCG as a force multiplier and a good step towards more intensive cooperation with the Air Force. Counter Drugs All three ships were deployed under both the flag of KW CARIB and for CTG 4.4 and were very successful during these periods. In cooperation with international units, CTG 4.4 and KWCARIB seized approximately 19,500 kg and 14,200 kg of contraband from the trade market respectively this year. Thus, 2022 is a record year. These international operations were conducted by KWCARIB in coordination with various countries including the United States, France, Colombia, and the United Kingdom in the US-led collaborative framework Joint Interagency Task Force South. Salute shots were fired upon the arrival of Zr.Ms. Friesland in Aruba.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.8)
sections.text: 7_Navy_Annual_Report_2022_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-8 137 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Hurricane Relief The hurricane season, which ran from June 1 to November 30, did not lead to large-scale deployments this year. During the passage of tropical storm Bonnie in the Windward Islands, the Marine Squadron CARIB (MSC), the Aruban Militia in Aruba (ARUMIL), as well as CIDW and CURMIL in Curaçao, were on standby and worked together with the local police during the passage. Additionally, the units provided small-scale assistance during the annual exercise Windward Express in Sint Maarten, Saba, and Sint Eustatius during the passage of tropical storm Fiona. Throughout the exercise, the military worked intensively with local authorities and aid organizations. Land Units The MSC, rotations of CIDW, and the Sint Maarten Detachment (DETSXM) completed a full and challenging readiness and training program. The MSC practiced Military Operations in Urban Terrain in the United States during Caribbean Urban Warrior. They also participated, together with the Boat Platoon and the Marine Detachment Sint Maarten, in the international exercise Tradewinds in Military of CurMil in Curaçao.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.9)
sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Belize and Mexico, where they practiced Riverine and Jungle operations. In August, the units received the long-awaited Improved Operational Soldier System package. In October, the international exercise Tres Kolos took place in Aruba, in which, alongside the French and Americans, all land units of CZMCARIB participated. DETSXM participated in the Commando Training in Martinique in November. The three rotations of CIDW were provided in 2022 by the 12th Infantry Battalion Air Assault Regiment of Heutsz and the 104th Reconnaissance Squadron Joint ISTAR Commando. During the rotations, they trained in Aruba, Curaçao, and Bonaire. Local authorities frequently utilized the CIDW search team. Additionally, CURMIL and ARUMIL took a first step in professionalization in 2022, based on the Ambition Document CZMCARIB. These units consist of personnel employed by the countries of Aruba and Curaçao and are directed by CZMCARIB. Military Assistance In 2022, CZMCARIB provided 24 soft and hard military assistance operations to the authorities of the countries and islands of the Kingdom. Some examples are described below: In January, CURMIL provided hard military assistance in Curaçao to enforce COVID-19 measures, including enforcing the curfew. In January, the Primary Healthcare Company opened a vaccination site at Marine Base Parera for booster vaccinations. The EOD supported the investigation into the cause of an explosion in Curaçao. In Bonaire and Curaçao, the search team assisted in searches of prisons, homes, plots, and vehicles. Among other things, phones, money, drugs, weapons, and documents were found. During the summer leave, CIDW assisted in Curaçao in the search for a missing Dutch tourist in Christoffelpark. During Tropical Storm Bonnie, CURMIL, CIDW, MSC, and ARUMIL provided assistance in Aruba and Curaçao. During Tropical Storm Fiona, MSC and DETSXM provided support in Sint Maarten, Saba, and Sint Eustatius. In Curaçao, CIDW conducted static observation twice at the request of the Public Prosecution Service. CURMIL collaborated with the local police during the harvest festival in Curaçao and performed traffic guidance tasks.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.10)
sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Visiting Units Throughout 2022, several units came to the Caribbean to conduct their training. Among others, NLMARSOF, other units of the Marine Corps, the Commando Troops, 43 Mechanized Brigade, and 101 Engineer Battalion utilized the Training Hub CARIB. Various courses were also offered, such as the sniper course, tropical medicine, diving training, and shooting training. Finally, several international partners came to the Caribbean for training and exercises, including the French and Americans. Directorate Control CZMCARIB Head: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) ing. P. Borsje-Senders, from August 1 Lieutenant Commander (kltz) M.C. Borsje-Senders handed over the position on August 1 to Lieutenant Commander M.C. Philipse-Breitenstein MSc Marines on exercise in Curacao.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.11)
sections.text: Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied Finance In 2022, the Finance department of CZMCARIB had a budget of 22.9 million euros, which was in accordance with the submitted budget. The final realization of the budget was 23.4 million euros, partly due to the currency claim of 4 million being paid by itself. The realization fell short due to limited travel opportunities as a result of COVID-19, but there were more business trips and training activities, including Caribbean Engineer, than in 2021. Due to a catch-up in training, 220% of this budget was realized. The country package still resulted in a 12.5% reduction in the salaries of local staff. Management Information In the area of Management Information, CZMCARIB made further progress in implementing the Business Intelligence and Improved Management Information dashboard for management information and reporting to CZSK. In the spring, the department published the information management plan CZMCARIB, the first information management plan of CZSK. The management also adjusted the annual plan for 2023 so that it aligns with the business reporting and is better secured internally. Marine Base Parera (MBPAR) Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) M.J.M. Hezemans MSc The year 2022 was marked by the end of the COVID-19 measures. This meant that MBPAR welcomed units again for exercises and that colleagues came on business trips to conduct audits or provide support in other ways. The many months of working from home, remote meetings, and maintaining distance affected the mutual bond. Therefore, the barracks invested a lot of energy in organizing joint activities in 2022. Booster location This year began with the establishment of a local COVID-19 booster vaccination site in the sports hall of MBPAR. On January 8, staff, their family members, and those of various partner government agencies were given the opportunity to receive their booster vaccination.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.12)
sections.text: Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied VLAC 2022 Until June, the base assisted the Curaçao Sail Foundation in organizing VLAC 2022; a four-yearly sailing event that lasted six days and is comparable to SAIL Amsterdam. From June 6 to June 12, CZMCARIB ensured that the Marine Band performed a continuous tattoo and that they performed for the public at Brionplein. Additionally, on Friday and Saturday, a defense village was open to the public at Motetwerf, where the Roadshow also contributed. On these days, they also provided demonstrations on land, in the air, and on the water. Film recordings Invasion Following VLAC, the filming of the movie 'Invasie' took place in Curaçao, Aruba, and Saba. Although the majority was coordinated by the Headquarters and Maritime Maintenance, the recordings took place with almost the entire crew on MBPAR. Lines Loose 2.0 In the past, a large party was regularly organized for all personnel of CZMCARIB and the Coast Guard in Curaçao. After a year full of effort, on December 9, Zr.Ms. Friesland and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan were moored at the Marinebasis Parera.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.13)
sections.text: Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied therefore organized the 'Trossen Los 2.0' party. With the help of various Truk’i’Pan and musical performances from, among others, the Sleeves, it was a successful evening. Other events On King's Day, the traditional Grand Parade was held. This time in the presence of C-ZSK. For the first time since the pandemic, there was an opportunity to celebrate Christmas together again. Military personnel and the local population attended mass together at the exercise area of the naval base. On New Year's Eve, the Pagara was also lit together while enjoying an oliebol and a drink. This million-firecracker is ignited annually in the days leading up to the new year to drive away evil spirits. Porto Mari Nature’s Walk & Run On September 4, the barracks organized the Nature’s Walk & Run event together with Porto Mari, where participants completed a course of 5 or 10 km in the rugged terrain near the beach of Porto Mari. Caribbeans Fittest The Sports Bureau organized the Caribbeans Fittest event in 2022 together with CrossFit Damacor and CrossFit Willemstad. The final took place on September 17 and 18 at MWC Brakkeput and MBPAR. Marines demonstrated a Fastrope action during VLAC.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.14)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean KLM Cityrun On November 26 and 27, the barracks supported the annual marathon of Curaçao. Participants could choose between the full and half marathon or run 5 or 10 kilometers. Heavy rainfall made this edition a true challenge, with runners sometimes having to wade through water several decimeters deep. Marine Barracks Suffisant (MKSUF) Commander: Major (majmarns) S. Baan This year, the barracks took new steps in facilitating the Royal Marechaussee. Many renovations on the premises were successfully completed in 2022. The delays caused by the pandemic were slowly being caught up due to a shortage of qualified personnel. The CURMIL welcomed its first female colleague in training. The Social Development Program started in a new format and was positioned alongside the regular training program as an ‘incubator’ for new talent and meaningful training for young people with a chance for a retake. The barracks could gradually count on additional budget to address its growth issues. This had a positive effect on the more than 500 personnel working there. Hats off and berets on! Caribbean marines completed the EMV at MKSUF.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.15)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Marine Barracks Savaneta Aruba (MSKSAV) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) B. van Beekhuizen Marine Barracks Savaneta is located in Aruba and houses the 32nd Marine Squadron (32RSQN) and the Aruban Militia. These consist of a staff, platoons, and support units. The Marine Squadron and the ARUMIL have various tasks. For this purpose, they train and exercise in the United States, French Guiana, Suriname, the French Caribbean islands, and the Windward and Leeward Islands. Noordam MSc General The support point further strengthened its relationships this year with the Emergency Operation Center, which is represented by various ministries. This was achieved through contributions to a Table Top training for disaster preparedness. FRISC’s in action during the exercise Très Kolos.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.16)
sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Throughout the year, plans for the construction of the new Naval Support Base seemed to take shape. The lease contract has been signed, and recently the RVB released the design sketch of the new barracks. The fencing that encloses the area was installed this year, and the space can be secured through a gate. Due to various issues, it appears that the new support base will experience delays. In collaboration with the Sint Maarten Police Corps, MSTPPB established a shooting range. All other safety partners on the island also made use of this facility. Despite some bureaucratic processes, the shooting range can now also be used for static shooting skills. Raiding Section (RS) In August, the RS, in a new composition, conducted a shooting training and the drivers obtained the necessary driving licenses for the new Anaconda vehicles. This was the unit's top priority. The RS participated in the exercise Barracuda Warrior together with the MSC. This was followed by the exercise Caribbean Urban Warrior at Camp Lejeune. During training, the unit learned combat techniques in Military Operations in Urban Terrain. The unique training location and opportunities that Camp Lejeune offers provided the team with experience in Three Block War. This was of added value for the training level and junior leadership of the unit. In the coming year, the RS also prepared for the hurricane season and participated in the exercises Hurricane Relief Exercise (HUREX) and Windward Express. In this context, the unit, together with the MSC, made further arrangements with local partners on the island regarding how to cooperate in the event of a possible hurricane passage. FRISC Section In the first quarter of 2022, there were various movements towards Saba and Sint Eustatius to transport equipment and personnel. Furthermore, the team supported the RS multiple times with exercises and assisted MSTPPB and Gonzalo. Events In 2022, unfortunately, there was no Marines run. This event usually takes place during the annual HUREX. However, this year Beat the Marines took place. Each year, there is more enthusiasm for this, causing the event to grow every year. The team also participated in many sports activities organized by Tri Sport on the island.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.17)
sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Support Vessel Zr.Ms. Pelikaan Commander: Lieutenant (ltz1) M.J.C. Jereskes MSc The year 2022 began for Zr.Ms. Pelikaan with a long period at the dock at MBPAR for the modernization of both the high and low classified networks. With support from the Netherlands from the DMI and the DMO, the hardware and software were modernized. By mid-February, the work was completed and the ship was free to move again. Due to the fact that some time had passed since the last training period, the leadership opted for an internal training period of two weeks. During this time, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan made a port visit to Tobago over the weekend to improve international relations. Due to strict COVID-19 measures, the leadership, in consultation with the Dutch ambassador in Port of Spain, chose a dinner instead of a reception. Dignitaries from Trinidad & Tobago were present, including representatives from the coast guard, armed forces, island government, and the crisis center for (natural) disasters. After the training period, the ship was in Curaçao from early March to mid-April for annual maintenance. During this period, technicians renewed the satellite communication system thanks to a temporary solution. Together with the previous maintenance on the networks, this ended a period of many malfunctions that made operations and command and control difficult. The maintenance concluded with approval from the classification bureau Lloyds, the retrieval of the CIDW, and the sailing material tests. Zr.Ms. Pelikaan combined this with training to prepare the crew for conducting lifting operations with helicopters. The month of April ended with the ship serving as a sparring partner in the training trajectory of the station ship and providing ceremonial support during the King's Day festivities. The ship docked in the Annabaai and rendered a salute in honor of the King. In May, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan participated in the international exercise Tradewinds. This exercise focuses on increasing security in the Caribbean, with the United States taking a coaching and leading role. The role of host country rotates among countries in and around the Caribbean basin. This year, Belize was the host country for the Jungle track and Mexico for the Riverine and Maritime track. CZMCARIB sent to all

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.18)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean conducted three tracks with a delegation. Zr.Ms. Pelikaan transported the delegations of the MSC to Belize and Mexico from Aruba and participated in the Maritime track itself. During this, it made various port visits to the island of Cozumel and exercised with, among others, the Mexican and Canadian navies, the United States Coast Guard, and non-governmental organizations. After this, the ship visited the port of Progreso, where it supported a Dutch trade mission with a reception and tours for the ambassador in Mexico. In the period leading up to the summer, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan supported the filming of Seastate 9 during various sailing missions. The ship also participated in the VLAC, where it held an open house, provided logistical support for all military activities on site, and took the lead in the sail out. After the summer, the annual biweekly training period SARC 3 and 4 took place under MOST, during which Zr.Ms. Pelikaan made a port visit to Santa Marta and was ultimately declared operationally ready with a very satisfactory rating. In the month of September, the ship was moored in Cozumel during the exercise Exercise Tradewinds.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.19)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean executed the three-week exercise Windward Express in Sint Maarten, Saba, and Sint Eustatius. Here, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan provided transport between the islands and offered logistical support. In October, the ship was stationed near Curaçao for two weeks to provide amphibious and logistical support to the DDG. In November, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan participated in Suriname, just like in 2021, in the program surrounding the celebrations of Surinamese independence. In collaboration with the Dutch ambassador, a reception was organized for dignitaries from the Surinamese armed forces and government, as well as French and American partners in the region. The year concluded with the ship conducting transports for the CIDW to and from Bonaire and supporting the sniper training. Department of Material Maintenance Head: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) M.J. These incidents mostly occurred in the operational domain. In 2022, all docking and construction permits for Wacawa were issued by the ministries of Curaçao. They indicated that Defense had not properly managed the permits. This led to many discussions with the fishermen and the ministries. Safety Awareness and Safety Leadership Course In September, V&M was an important item on the agenda of the CARIB management meeting. In the second week of the month, various rounds took place, and the construction of a new facility for CIDW at Wacawa was on the agenda.

sections.text: 7_Navy_Annual_Report_2022_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-21 150 The Command of the Navy in the Caribbean reflected on how they deal with this theme and where improvements are possible. They considered how laws and regulations are applied in daily work. To conclude that week, a two-day Safety Leadership Course was held for various commanders and department heads from Curaçao, Aruba, and Sint Maarten. This training focused on the role of the commander regarding safety in a broad sense: reporting and investigating incidents and applying risk management. Department of Organizational Social Work (DBMW) region CARIB Team Leader: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) H.J.H. Goetzee The main tasks that Organizational Social Work (BMW) performs in the Caribbean region are assistance, service provision, reporting, support after traumatic events, and crisis intervention. For the CARIB region, BMW, together with the Spiritual Care Services and in Aruba also with HR, is responsible for notifying family announcements. With the lifting of COVID-19 restrictions during the year, it was again possible to conduct work visits to Bonaire and Sint Maarten. Here, colleagues from the Royal Marechaussee and DBMW work to be more accessible to this personnel and their families on these islands and to provide better assistance and services. Additionally, there were also more work visitors from the Netherlands. In January, the National (Veterans) Ombudsman R. van Zutphen visited Curaçao. He spoke with the team leader about veterans' cases on the islands and had a joint meeting in Curaçao and Aruba with post-active veterans. In March, a sailor working on MBPAR died as a result of a tragic traffic accident. Together with colleagues from the Spiritual Care Services (DGV), BMW CARIB supported the bereaved family members who came to Curaçao and guided them. Care was also provided for the direct colleagues. On April 26, Lieutenant at Sea 1 H.J.H. Goetzee received a royal decoration from the governor of Curaçao on behalf of the Royal Netherlands Navy in cooperation with the Department of BMW.

sections.text: 7_KM_Annual_Report_2022_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-23 152 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean DMO/JIVC CARIB Team Leader: Lieutenant (ltz2) T. van der Wereld General During the projects in the second half of 2021 and early 2022, it became clear that it was no longer desirable to leave the position of JIVC team leader CARIB unfilled. Starting in July, Lieutenant at Sea 2 T. van der Wereld returned from the Netherlands to take on this role. This completed the staffing. Projects To facilitate the renovation of the cafeteria on the MKSAV, an adjustment to the fiber optic network infrastructure and the main cluster point was necessary. Since preparations for a complete replacement of the fiber optic infrastructure at various barracks in the Caribbean were already in the planning stages, the team chose to start the installation of the new fiber optic ring at MKSAV and to relocate the main cluster point. Furthermore, the team made various adjustments to the network connections between the Caribbean and the Netherlands with the providers. This increased the reliability and availability of the Defense IT network in the CARIB and reduced the impact of disruptions from civilian network suppliers. In the fourth quarter, the department made the final preparations to commence the complete renewal of the highly classified networks in the Caribbean in 2023. This will allow CZSK CARIB to transfer local management of these networks to JIVC CARIB, aligning with the current working methods in the Netherlands. Drug seizures as a result of the collaboration between Zr.Ms. Groningen and the Coast Guard.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.24)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Coast Guard Caribbean Director Coast Guard: Brigadier General (briggenmarns) F.O. Boots Deputy Director Coast Guard: E.H.G. Middelhof MBA The environment in which the Coast Guard operated in the Caribbean this year partly determined the priorities and deployment of its capabilities. Several factors underpinned the physically delivered output by the units and the results achieved. Venezuela Due to the unstable situation in Venezuela, the Coast Guard also monitored developments in that country in 2022. At the end of the year, discussions were set to begin regarding the reopening of the borders between Venezuela and the Windward Islands. Initially, this would concern the maritime borders for the transport of goods such as food. However, the discussions did not take place. In 2022, the Coast Guard saw an increase in the number of undocumented individuals from Venezuela; this year, 170 persons attempted to enter the islands illegally. Drug Smuggling The Coast Guard made several significant drug seizures in 2022, either in collaboration with Defense or third parties, intercepting 29,274 kg of cocaine and 5,116 kg of marijuana and hemp. Several chain partners with whom intensive cooperation took place in 2022 included CTG 4.4, SSCG, USCG, and the American Joint Inter Agency Task Force-South. Cooperation in 2022 varied from initial detection by flying units of the Coast Guard to joint operations and the use of the service's powers in international waters under the San José Treaty. Search and Rescue Cases In 2022, the Coast Guard rescued 598 persons from emergency situations. The service itself recorded 46 deceased and 11 missing persons in its area of responsibility. COVID-19 The Omicron wave of COVID-19 infections reached the Caribbean region in early 2022 and, like previous variants of the virus, also impacted the Coast Guard. This resulted in a temporarily reduced operational availability of operational units. Additionally, several planned initiatives for early 2022 could not be realized.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.25)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Cooperation with Defense The structural cooperation with Defense is described in a covenant between the CZSK and the Coast Guard. The covenant outlines mutual support in the form of personnel, resources, and services, and implements the management task by Defense and the execution by the Coast Guard, as established in the National Coast Guard Act. In 2022, this was also put into practice, and the cooperation was positive. The SSCG was available to the Coast Guard in 2022, in accordance with the operational availability of the ship. However, this meant that the vessel was deployed less in 2022 compared to the number of sailing days established in the covenant. This distribution was agreed upon by the Coast Guard in consultation with Defense. Successively, Zr.Ms. Holland, Zr.Ms. Groningen, and again Zr.Ms. Holland served as SSCG in 2022. Equipment In 2022, the Coast Guard completed the replacement of the shore radar chain in the Windward Islands. After the installation of the last two new masts (the other six had been installed earlier), a Marine fires at the shooting range with a MAG medium machine gun.

sections.title: Bijlagen Colofon 19 12 2022 Schepen (p.3)
sections.text: The attachments from July (unfortunately coinciding with the Navy Days) were won by the cadets. A remarkable athletic achievement. The evening before the grand swearing-in ceremony, the now traditional Marine Band concert took place. This event was held outdoors and is intended for the parents of the cadets, staff of the KIM, and their partners. On Friday, June 30, the grand swearing-in ceremony took place, where a total of 84 young officers took the oath or made a promise. Following this, in the afternoon, the officers' diplomas were awarded. In 2022, as is customary, a KIM delegation participated in the Nijmegen Four Days March. Immediately after the summer leave, on Monday, August 29, the 2022 promotion arrived at the institute and departed after a short introduction for the Maritime Introduction Period to Texel. This was followed by a boat trip and sailing on the magnificent Norwegian sailing ship Statsrad Lemkuhl. The inauguration took place on September 21, and the ponjaard was awarded to them, allowing them to be installed as cadets on Friday, September 23. To strengthen the connection with the residents of Den Helder, the KIM held the KVMO-Winnubst concert this year on November 15. This was possible for the first time in two years. This tradition is a free concert by the music association Winnubst. They make an important contribution to the socio-cultural life in Den Helder and within the region. The harmony orchestra consists of advanced musicians. Every year, in the second half of December, the Assaut takes place at the KIM. The Assaut is a tradition that dates back to 1871. The Corps of cadets transforms 't Zaaltje and the surrounding areas into a richly decorated gala; each year with a different theme. The Corps of cadets works 24 hours a day in two shifts during this period to realize this theme. Originally, the Assaut was established by the Cadet Fencing Association Olympia as a fencing tournament, but it has since evolved into a three-day gala that returns annually. In 2022, the Assaut had the theme "Arabian Nights." For two years, the grand gala ball of the KIM could not take place, but from December 15 to 17, it finally happened again. The Assaut featured three festive evenings. On the first evening, the Pre-Assaut took place, during which the Corps of cadets thanked the parents and permanent staff for all the support they provided throughout the year. The second evening is dedicated to the Gala Ball. The final evening is the Corps Assaut, an evening for the Corps of cadets.
